extracted.intended_audience: conference organizers, program chairs, area chairs, and reviewers for machine-learning conferences (e.g., ICML)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical findings about designing and operating peer review for large machine-learning conferences, covering reviewer recruitment, assignment, discussion management, anonymity policies, and decision rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers give systematically lower scores when told a submission is a resubmission (almost one point lower on a 10-point Likert overall evaluation); narrower criteria like “Paper Quality” are especially underrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for a trade-off between discouraging resubmissions and introducing unfairness. One mitigation is to postpone revealing resubmission history until after reviewers submit their initial reviews. Also consider these effects when deciding whether to make reviews of rejected papers publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herding in reviewer discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the order in which reviewers join a discussion (e.g., most-positive-first vs most-negative-first) biases the final decision (herding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomized trial at ICML 2020 (≈1,500 papers) found no statistically significant evidence of herding in the discussion phase. Implication: no special countermeasures appear necessary for discussion-order herding in asynchronous conference discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novice reviewer recruiting (selection + mentoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can very junior reviewers be recruited and guided so they enlarge the reviewer pool without compromising review quality? Approach: select strong junior reviewers from auxiliary reviews and provide a senior mentor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICML experiment: invite top-performing junior reviewers and pair them with senior mentors; measure quality via area-chair ratings. Result: combined selection and mentoring produced reviews at least comparable, and on some metrics superior, to the conventional pool (e.g., 30% of experimental reviews exceeded expectations vs 14% for main pool). Recommendation: replicate at larger scale and evaluate components separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind review to reduce identity-based bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealing author identities from reviewers aims to prevent factors other than scientific quality (prestige, country, gender, race, institutional affiliation) from influencing reviews and to promote the perception of fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence shows double-blind review can increase representation of women and reduce prestige effects (the Matthew effect). However, perfect blindness is often impossible: studies show reviewers correctly guess authors/institutions only ~25–42% of the time; common unblinding clues include self-references and explicit data-source statements. Journals/conferences can reduce unblinding by policy and manuscript requirements. Double-blind also has symbolic benefits for perceived fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of specific bias modes (prestige, country, gender, race, stereotype threat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of bias that can affect peer review: Matthew effect (prestige/familiarity), country-of-origin bias, gender bias, race-related disparities (e.g., in grant funding), and potential stereotype threat effects on authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design review policies (e.g., double-blind review) and empirical monitoring to mitigate these biases. Recognize that some biases are implicit and not conscious; policy changes may reduce both real bias and perception of unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer/paper assignment quality (affinity matrix and failure modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good reviewer-paper matching is essential; failure modes include low-quality affinity graphs and constraints that leave papers orphaned or poorly matched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve affinity data via bidding, blended assignment approaches, and allow area chairs to find reviewers outside automated assignments. Consider optimizing alternate objectives (e.g., product of affinities instead of sum) and monitor for orphaned or low-affinity assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid single-person reviewer selection that yields like-minded panels
rubrics_metrics.description: When one person (e.g., an area chair) picks reviewers from their own crowd, the resulting reviewer set may be homogenous and non-representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blended assignment: automated constraints for first reviewers, assign two ACs per paper, then have ACs find additional reviewers to reduce like-mindedness and diagnose misassignments early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce reviewer anchoring and dominance effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Review anchoring (early opinions setting the tone) and dominance by loud/charismatic reviewers can bias outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard conference process where reviews are hidden until completion reduces anchoring. Asynchronous/non-meeting-based discussions reduce dominance effects compared to in-person PC meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize reviewer load and encourage review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: High reviewer workload and time pressure lead to low-quality reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize average reviewer load, consider staggered deadlines, provide incentives/motivation (see below), and use bidding to allocate reviewers where they have expertise to reduce time/per-review cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve reviewer motivation (transparency and author feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Low motivation produces low-quality reviews; lack of accountability can permit poor reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make reviewers visible to each other (reduce full anonymity among reviewers) and enable author feedback channels so authors can point out poor reviews. Publishing submissions nonanonymously after an initial period may also increase reviewer accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow author communication (author response) to reduce miscommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: Miscommunications (typos, unclear exposition) can cause poor reviews; the author response can clarify and change reviewer opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an author-feedback stage (author response) and make it an explicit part of the pipeline; many reviewers report that author responses and discussions change their opinions (author response preferred by most).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent dictatorship in decision-making (defined power approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid giving single actors (ACs or PCs) unilateral override power that can create arbitrary accept/reject outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a defined power rule: if reviewers agree, that decision holds; if reviewers disagree, ask area chairs to decide; only involve program chairs when ACs disagree. This limits arbitrary overrides while keeping escalation paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative reviewing objective: 'Are there a significant number of people who will be interested?'
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic acceptance test: accept papers for which a significant number of community members will be interested; aim to minimize approximation error when sampling reviewers to estimate this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because querying the entire community is infeasible, design reviewer selection and assignment to approximate community interest with minimal error. Ensure reviewer pools and matching are diverse and representative to reduce approximation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bidding and blended assignment to improve affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect reviewer bids to improve the affinity matrix before automated assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine bidding with constrained automated assignment and allow AC intervention to find suitable reviewers. This raises the quality of initial assignments and enables handling of edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational measures: assign two area chairs and an early first reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational choices that improve assignment robustness: assign two ACs per paper and constrain the system to assign a first reviewer in a less-constrained manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First reviewer chosen by the constrained system tends to be higher-quality; ACs locating reviewers flags misassignments early, and ACs can recruit outside the PC where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow appendices/ancillary materials (optional for reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can include appendices so complex ideas are fully communicated, but mandatory consumption increases reviewer burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit appendices/ancillary materials but make reading them optional for reviewers to balance completeness vs reviewer time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reviews as a learning and accountability tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Open reviews enable learning from other reviews and allow more natural author responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reviews and double-blind review are not mutually exclusive: hide authors for an initial review period (e.g., ~2 months) and then reveal identities or make reviews public afterward to combine benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision thresholds based on average reviewer score (practical mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical mapping at ICML: average review score < 2.2 → ~0% acceptance; > 3.1 → ~100% acceptance; intermediate averages (≈2.33, 2.67, 3.0) correspond to graded probabilities and common reviewer combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such empirical thresholds as decision heuristics but recognize discretization and reviewer variance; handle borderline cases with discussion, AC judgment, and escalation rules rather than rigid cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote independence in reviewer assignment to reduce variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlated reviewer assignment increases decision variance; independent reviewer samples give more reliable estimates of a paper's intrinsic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assignment algorithms to reduce correlated reviewer selection; aim for multiple relatively independent reviewers (three samples) and use discussion/author feedback to reduce variance further (observed SD dropped from 0.64 to 0.51 after discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and monitor reviewer/review quality (area-chair ratings & metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess reviews via area-chair ratings and other performance metrics to identify strong or weak reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experimental selection (e.g., select junior reviewers who produced the strongest reviews in an auxiliary process) and track metrics such as proportion of reviews 'exceeding expectations' to inform recruiting and mentoring decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine policy experiments with careful empirical evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing review policy (resubmission disclosure, herding mitigation, novice reviewer programs), run controlled experiments and analyze outcomes statistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICML implemented randomized trials and auxiliary review processes with statistical analysis; conference organizers should similarly pilot changes, collect data (e.g., acceptance rates, review scores, AC ratings), and publish or act on findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make trade-offs explicit when choosing review policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Every policy (double-blind, open review, allowing appendices, recruiting novices) has costs and benefits that affect bias, reviewer motivation, and workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate trade-offs explicitly (e.g., double-blind reduces bias but may reduce reviewer motivation) and consider hybrid approaches (temporary anonymity, mentoring) to balance competing goals.
